skeleton.name: Skeleton
skeleton.summary: Bones and cartilage: the body's load-bearing frame.
skeleton.overview: The adult skeleton has 206 bones plus the cartilages that cap joints, join the ribs to the sternum and shape the nose and airway. It is organised into an axial skeleton (skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum) that protects the brain, spinal cord, heart and lungs, and an appendicular skeleton (the limbs with their girdles) built for movement. Bone is living tissue: it remodels throughout life in response to load, stores calcium and phosphate, and houses the marrow that makes blood cells.
functions: Supports the body and gives it shape
Protects the brain, spinal cord and thoracic organs
Provides levers and attachment points for muscles
Stores calcium and phosphate
Houses red marrow, the site of blood cell production
clinical: Fractures follow trauma or weakened bone (osteoporosis)
Osteoarthritis wears the articular cartilage of weight-bearing joints
Scoliosis, kyphosis and disc disease affect the vertebral column

joints.name: Joints & ligaments
joints.summary: Ligaments, joint capsules, discs and membranes that bind the skeleton.
joints.overview: Where bones meet, connective tissue holds them together and limits their motion. Ligaments are dense bands of collagen running bone to bone; intervertebral discs are fibrocartilage cushions between vertebral bodies; interosseous membranes bind the paired bones of the forearm and leg. BodyParts3D models a selection of these structures, including every intervertebral disc, the plantar ligaments of the foot and the check ligaments of the eye muscles.
functions: Stabilise joints while allowing controlled movement
Absorb and distribute load between bones
Transmit forces along the limbs
clinical: Ligament sprains and tears (for example the knee's cruciate ligaments)
Herniated intervertebral discs can compress nerve roots
Degenerative disc disease narrows the space between vertebrae

teeth.name: Teeth
teeth.summary: The permanent dentition: 32 teeth of the upper and lower jaws.
teeth.overview: Adults have up to 32 permanent teeth: in each quadrant two incisors, one canine, two premolars and three molars. Incisors cut, canines tear, premolars and molars grind. Each tooth has a crown covered by enamel, the hardest tissue in the body, a root anchored in the jaw by the periodontal ligament, and a pulp cavity carrying vessels and nerves. This model includes 28 teeth; the third molars (wisdom teeth) are absent.
functions: Cut, tear and grind food to begin digestion
Support speech and the shape of the face
clinical: Dental caries dissolves enamel and dentine
Periodontal disease loosens the tooth's attachment
Impacted wisdom teeth are a common reason for extraction

muscles.name: Muscles
muscles.summary: Skeletal muscles, tendons and aponeuroses that move the body.
muscles.overview: Skeletal muscle makes up roughly 40% of body mass. Each muscle spans one or more joints, attaching to bone through tendons or flat aponeuroses; when its fibres shorten it pulls the bones together. Muscles work in groups: agonists produce a movement, antagonists control it, and stabilisers hold neighbouring joints still. The model includes the muscles of the limbs, trunk, neck, face, larynx and pharynx, and the diaphragm.
functions: Produce movement and maintain posture
Stabilise joints
Drive breathing (diaphragm and intercostals)
Generate heat
clinical: Strains and tears from overload
Compartment syndrome when pressure rises within a fascial compartment
Muscular dystrophies progressively weaken muscle fibres

heart.name: Heart
heart.summary: Chambers, valves and walls of the heart, with the pericardium.
heart.overview: The heart is a four-chambered muscular pump about the size of a fist. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the venae cavae and passes it through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle, which pumps it to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns to the left atrium, crosses the mitral valve into the thick-walled left ventricle and is ejected through the aortic valve into the aorta. The model separates the atrial and ventricular walls, the chambers, the valve leaflets and cusps, and the papillary muscles that anchor the mitral and tricuspid valves.
functions: Pump blood through the pulmonary and systemic circulations
Keep blood flowing one way with four valves
Generate its own rhythm through the conduction system
clinical: Coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction
Heart failure when the ventricles cannot pump enough
Valve disease: stenosis or regurgitation
Arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation
keyStructures: Anterior papillary muscle of right ventricle

arteries.name: Arteries
arteries.summary: Systemic and pulmonary arteries carrying blood away from the heart.
arteries.overview: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under pressure. The aorta leaves the left ventricle, arches over the heart giving off the vessels to the head and arms, then descends through the thorax and abdomen before dividing into the iliac arteries for the pelvis and legs. The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. With 642 modelled pieces, this is the largest layer in the atlas, down to the segmental arteries of the lungs, liver and kidneys and the small branches on the surface of the brain.
functions: Distribute oxygenated blood to every organ
Regulate blood pressure and flow through muscular walls
Carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs (pulmonary arteries)
clinical: Atherosclerosis narrows arteries and can cause heart attack or stroke
Aneurysms are dangerous dilatations, most often of the abdominal aorta
Peripheral arterial disease limits blood flow to the legs

veins.name: Veins
veins.summary: Systemic and pulmonary veins returning blood to the heart.
veins.overview: Veins return blood to the heart at low pressure, helped by valves and by the squeeze of surrounding muscles. Deep veins run alongside the arteries; superficial veins such as the cephalic, basilic and saphenous veins lie just under the skin. Blood from the gut drains first to the liver through the hepatic portal vein before joining the inferior vena cava. The pulmonary veins are the exception to the rule: they carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
functions: Return blood to the heart
Act as a reservoir holding most of the blood volume
Route nutrient-rich blood from the gut through the liver (portal system)
clinical: Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism
Varicose veins from failing valves in the superficial veins
Portal hypertension in liver disease

nervous.name: Nervous system
nervous.summary: Brain, spinal cord, cranial and spinal nerves, ganglia and meninges.
nervous.overview: The nervous system gathers information, decides and commands. The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system; the cranial and spinal nerves with their ganglia form the peripheral nervous system. This model is richest in the head: the cerebral gyri and lobes, the basal ganglia, thalamus and hypothalamus, the brainstem and cerebellum, the ventricles, the optic pathway and the nerves of the orbit. Peripheral nerves of the limbs are not part of this BodyParts3D release.
functions: Sense the environment and the body's internal state
Integrate information, memory and emotion
Control voluntary and involuntary movement
Regulate organs through the autonomic system
clinical: Stroke: loss of blood supply to part of the brain
Epilepsy, migraine and neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's
Nerve compression syndromes and neuropathies

sensory.name: Sensory organs
sensory.summary: Eyes and ears with their internal structures.
sensory.overview: The eye focuses light through the cornea and lens onto the retina, whose signals travel along the optic nerve to the brain. The model separates the cornea, sclera, choroid, iris, lens, vitreous body and retina, plus the lacrimal apparatus that produces and drains tears and the tarsal plates of the eyelids. The external ear collects sound towards the tympanic membrane; the middle and inner ear are not modelled in this release.
functions: Vision: focusing and detecting light
Protecting and lubricating the eye (eyelids, tears)
Hearing and balance (ear)
clinical: Refractive errors, cataract and glaucoma
Retinal detachment and macular degeneration
Conjunctivitis and blocked tear ducts

respiratory.name: Respiratory
respiratory.summary: Nose, larynx, trachea, bronchial tree and lungs.
respiratory.overview: Air enters through the nose, where cartilages support the nostrils and conchae warm and moisten it, passes the larynx, which guards the airway and produces the voice, and descends the trachea. The trachea divides into the main bronchi, which branch again and again into the segmental bronchial trees modelled here, one for each bronchopulmonary segment. Gas exchange takes place in the alveoli at the end of this tree; the lung tissue itself is not a separate piece in this dataset, so the bronchial trees stand in for the lungs.
functions: Bring oxygen into the blood and remove carbon dioxide
Filter, warm and humidify inhaled air
Produce the voice (larynx)
Help regulate blood acidity
clinical: Asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease narrow the airways
Pneumonia infects the alveoli
Lung cancer most often arises in the bronchi

digestive.name: Digestive
digestive.summary: Mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, intestines, liver, pancreas.
digestive.overview: The digestive tract is a nine-metre tube from mouth to anus. Food is chewed, swallowed down the oesophagus, churned with acid in the stomach, digested and absorbed along the small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum), and its residue concentrated in the colon. The liver, gallbladder and pancreas pour bile and enzymes into the duodenum. The model includes the tongue, salivary glands and gums, the stomach and intestines in many segments, the liver as eight hepatovenous segments with its bile ducts, the gallbladder, the pancreas and the mesenteries that suspend the gut.
functions: Break food down mechanically and chemically
Absorb nutrients and water
Store and release energy (liver)
Eliminate waste
clinical: Reflux, gastritis and peptic ulcers
Appendicitis, inflammatory bowel disease and colorectal cancer
Gallstones, hepatitis and pancreatitis

urinary.name: Urinary
urinary.overview: The two kidneys filter about 180 litres of plasma a day, returning almost all of it to the blood and excreting the rest as urine. Urine drains through the ureters into the bladder, a muscular reservoir that empties through the urethra. The kidneys also regulate blood pressure, red cell production and vitamin D activation.
functions: Filter waste from the blood
Balance water, salts and acidity
Regulate blood pressure
Store and expel urine
clinical: Urinary tract infections
Kidney stones
Chronic kidney disease and dialysis

reproductive.name: Reproductive
reproductive.overview: BodyParts3D is built on an adult male, so this layer contains the male reproductive organs: the testes, which produce sperm and testosterone, the epididymis where sperm mature, the deferent ducts that carry them to the urethra, the seminal vesicles and prostate that add most of the seminal fluid, and the erectile bodies of the penis.
functions: Produce sperm and sex hormones
Deliver sperm and seminal fluid
clinical: Benign prostatic enlargement and prostate cancer
Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency
Inguinal hernias track along the spermatic cord

endocrine.name: Endocrine
endocrine.summary: Hormone-producing glands: thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, pineal.
endocrine.overview: Endocrine glands release hormones into the blood to regulate metabolism, growth, stress responses and reproduction. The pituitary, hanging from the base of the brain, controls most other glands. The adrenal glands cap the kidneys, producing cortisol, aldosterone and adrenaline. The pineal body, which sets the sleep-wake rhythm, is modelled with the brain; the thyroid gland is not included in this release.
functions: Coordinate metabolism, growth and stress responses
Regulate salt, water and blood pressure (adrenal cortex)
Control other glands (pituitary)
clinical: Diabetes mellitus
Thyroid over- and under-activity
Adrenal insufficiency and Cushing's syndrome

lymphatic.name: Lymphatic & immune
lymphatic.overview: Lymphatic vessels return tissue fluid to the blood and carry it through lymph nodes where immune cells inspect it. The spleen filters blood, recycles old red cells and mounts immune responses; the thymus, large in childhood, trains T lymphocytes. This release models the spleen and the two lobes of the thymus; lymph nodes and lymphatic vessels are not included.
functions: Return tissue fluid to the circulation
Filter blood and lymph
Produce and mature immune cells
clinical: Lymphoma and leukaemia
Splenic rupture after abdominal trauma
Lymphoedema when drainage is blocked

skin.name: Skin
skin.overview: The skin is the body's largest organ, about two square metres of barrier against infection, injury and water loss. Its outer epidermis constantly renews; the dermis beneath carries vessels, nerves, glands and hair follicles. In the atlas the skin is a single surface shown as a translucent overlay so the structures beneath stay visible; hair of the head, eyebrows and pubic hair are separate pieces.
functions: Protect against infection, injury and dehydration
Sense touch, pressure, temperature and pain
Regulate body temperature through sweat and blood flow
Make vitamin D
clinical: Eczema, psoriasis and acne
Skin cancers, including melanoma
Burns and wound healing
